# The Cost-effectiveness of Semaglutide and Tirzepatide for Patients with Knee Osteoarthritis and Obesity

**Authors:** Daniel J. Betensky; Karen C. Smith; Jeffrey N. Katz; Catherine Yang; David J. Hunter; Jamie E. Collins; Candace H. Feldman; Stephen P. Messier; Jason S. Kim; Faith Selzer; A. David Paltiel; Elena Losina

**Affiliations:** 1.Policy and Innovation eValuation in Orthopaedic Treatments (PIVOT) Center, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 2.Orthopaedic and Arthritis Center for Outcomes Research (OrACORe), Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 3.Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 4.J.B. Snow Biomechanics Laboratory, Department of Health and Exercise Science, Wake Forest University, Winston-Salem, NC, USA | 5.Rheumatology Department, Royal North Shore Hospital and Sydney Musculoskeletal Health, Kolling Institute, University of Sydney, Sydney, Australia | 6.Section of Clinical Sciences, Division of Rheumatology, Inflammation and Immunity, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 7.Departments of Epidemiology and Environmental Health, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 8.Department of Biostatistics, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA | 9.Arthritis Foundation, Atlanta, GA, USA | 10.Public Health Modeling Unit, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, USA

## Abstract

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RAs) lead to substantial weight-loss and pain reduction in persons with knee osteoarthritis (OA) and obesity.

Evaluate the cost-effectiveness of two GLP1RAs, semaglutide and tirzepatide for patients with OA and obesity.

Osteoarthritis Policy (OAPol) Model, a validated microsimulation model of knee OA, to estimate lifetime benefits and costs of weight-loss strategies.

Published data to derive treatment-related weight-loss, pain reduction and costs of GLP1RAs from the US Office of Health Policy.

Persons with knee OA and obesity in the US. The base case cohort had a Western Ontario McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) pain (0–100, 100 worst) of 71 and mean BMI of 40 kg/m2.

Lifetime

Healthcare, Societal

Semaglutide,tirzepatide, Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy (LSG), Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB), Diet and Exercise

Quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), cost, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICER).

Tirzepatide provided greater health benefits at lower costs than semaglutide and yielded a $57,400/QALY ICER vs. diet and exercise. For those eligible, RYGB provided greater health benefits at lower costs than the 2 GLP1RAs and had a $30,700/QALY ICER vs. LSG.

Tirzepatide’s ICER was most sensitive to changes in medication costs, treatment efficacy, and cohort baseline BMI. Tirzepatide and semaglutide had a 64% and semaglutide had a 34% probability of being cost-effective at a $100,000/QALY threshold.

Data from multiple sources.

Both tirzepatide and semaglutide would be widely considered cost-effective when compared directly to usual care. Tirzepatide would offer the most favorable return on investment to decision makers whose cost-effectiveness thresholds exceed $57,400/QALY.

The Arthritis Foundation and National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases.

## Introduction

Nearly 30 million US adults and 370 million individuals worldwide have knee osteoarthritis (OA) (1). Obesity increases the risk of developing knee OA (2–5). People with obesity are diagnosed with OA earlier and present with more severe pain and functional limitations than those without obesity (6–9).

Weight-loss reduces knee joint loading, systemic inflammation and knee pain (10–13). Weight-loss interventions include lifestyle approaches (diet and exercise), pharmaceuticals, and bariatric surgery. While diet and exercise can lead to clinically meaningful (>10%) weight-loss and pain reduction, bariatric surgery may provide more substantial weight-loss and additional health benefits like remission of type 2 diabetes (10, 12–14). It has previously been shown that diet and exercise and bariatric surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy) could offer good value for patients with knee OA and obesity when added to usual OA care (15–18).

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RAs, e.g., semaglutide and tirzepatide) were approved by the FDA in 2021 and 2023, respectively, as pharmacological weight-loss interventions and have become widely used (19–22). Semaglutide has been shown to reduce knee pain in individuals with OA (23). However, GLP1RAs are notably expensive (24). Given the clinical benefits and expense of GLP1RAs, we sought to define the circumstances – including clinical efficacies, treatment costs, and availability of alternative treatments – under which each GLP1RA approach to knee OA and obesity management might be cost-effective.

## Methods

### Analytic Overview

We used the Osteoarthritis Policy (OAPol) model, a validated and widely published Monte Carlo microsimulation of knee OA (15–18, 25–27), to assess the cost-effectiveness of semaglutide, tirzepatide, and other common weight-loss interventions in patients with knee OA and obesity. Primary outcomes were lifetime quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), medical costs (2024 USD), and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). We calculated ICERs as the ratio of the difference in lifetime costs and the corresponding difference in QALYs between two treatment strategies. We compared weight-loss interventions incrementally (calculated for adjacent strategies ranked by increasing costs) and against a single common comparator (usual care or diet and exercise). To distinguish between the two comparisons, we refer to ratios calculated against a common comparator as absolute cost-effectiveness ratios and ratios calculated incrementally with all strategies as ICERs.

Consistent with cost-effectiveness guidelines (28), a “dominated” strategy represents a less effective and more costly option than its alternatives. Compared to commonly accepted thresholds of $100,000/QALY in the United States (29–31), we defined the strategies “cost-effective” when their ICER (versus the next least costly, non-dominated alternative) remained below the $100,000/QALY threshold. Within the set of cost-effective options, we defined the optimal strategy for a given cost-effectiveness threshold as the strategy that delivers the largest additional health benefit while still meeting the threshold.(32) We also reported ICERs for each strategy to allow decision makers with varying thresholds to determine if a strategy would be cost-effective in their context.

We discounted costs and benefits at 3% annually (28). We conducted the base case evaluation from the healthcare perspective, which assesses only direct medical costs associated with treatment, and the societal perspective, which also evaluates indirect costs from OA pain and total knee replacement (TKR) (28). We conducted a primary analysis without bariatric surgeries available and a secondary analysis including them, given their differing clinical eligibility criteria from GLP1RAs and low utilization even among eligible patients (33). We also performed sensitivity analyses to examine robustness of our results to uncertainty in input parameters.

### Clinical Strategies Under Consideration

We examined six clinical strategies: 1) usual care (UC), 2) UC + diet and exercise, 3) UC + semaglutide, 4) UC + tirzepatide, 5) UC + laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG), and 6) UC + Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB). The UC, diet and exercise, and bariatric surgery regimens have been described in prior publications (15–18, 25–27). We present weight-loss regimen details in the Supplementary Material (SM, Sections 1.2B–F). All weight-loss interventions occurred alongside usual OA care.

### The OAPol Model Structure

The OAPol model is a Monte Carlo state-transition microsimulation of knee OA and its care (15–18, 25–27). The model initializes individuals with user-defined demographic (e.g. age, sex) and clinical (BMI, knee OA structural severity, comorbidities) characteristics. We derived model parameters from the STEP-9 study, a phase III trial of semaglutide in people with OA (Table 1) (23). The model uses 12-month cycles to update an individual’s health state, defined by obesity class, comorbidities and OA severity (Figure 1). In each health state, individuals accumulate costs and QALYs. We derived background costs from the 2020 CMS-HCC community model and 2017–2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data and indirect costs from data on workhours lost from knee pain (34–37). Each health state has an associated quality of life (QoL) utility that ranges from 0.0 (death) to 1.0 (perfect health). QoL utility depends on obesity, OA severity, knee pain, age and comorbidities. We derived utility weights using data from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) (38).

Treatment can improve QoL and reduce costs, but treatment-related adverse events may lead to additional costs and mortality. The uptake of OA treatments (NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections, opioids, TKR and revision TKR) depends on pain levels, interventions offered, and acceptance rates (SM, 1.2A). The model sets mortality using age/sex/race stratified 2020 US lifetables (39). Mortality rates are elevated for individuals with obesity, cardiovascular disease and cancer (SM, Table A2).

### Modeling Weight-loss Regimens

In OAPol, weight-loss regimens impact BMI, which in turn affects knee pain and may impact type 2 diabetes status. For everyone on a weight-loss regimen, the model assigns a BMI and pain reduction level along with a probability of adverse events, based on published clinical trial data or secondary analyses of data from randomized clinical trials. Weight-loss occurs over the course of two years. For the surgical strategies, an individual may maintain their weight-loss entirely or regain some part of the lost weight, over the remainder of their lifetime (SM, Table A8). For GLP1RA strategies, individuals maintain weight-loss for the duration of the treatment, and upon discontinuation gradually return to baseline weight over the course of two years.

Based on published results from a randomized trial, published results from observational studies, and our own secondary analysis of data from the WE-CAN study, we assumed a non-linear dose-response relationship to model the reduction in knee pain resulting from a weight-loss regimen, depending on the user-prespecified groups of BMI reduction (9, 40, 41). Pain benefits may be sustained or lost concordant with weight-loss duration.

Weight-loss interventions may additionally lead to remission and reduced incidence of diabetes. They can also reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs – stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiovascular-related death). Experiencing a MACE causes weight-loss treatment discontinuation and increased costs in subsequent cycles. After weight-loss regimen discontinuation, any reduced risk of MACEs reverts to baseline (SM, 1.1D).

### Model Inputs

#### Cohort Characteristics (Table 1)

In the base case, we focused on individuals with knee OA and obesity representative of a real-world population that could benefit from weight-loss interventions, using demographic and clinical data from STEP-9 (23). The resulting cohort was 81.6% female, 88.9% White non-Hispanic, with a mean age 56 years (SD 10.0), and a mean BMI 40.3 kg/m2 (7.2) (Table 1). The mean starting pain was 70.9 on the Western Ontario McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC; 0–100, 100 worst) (23). We derived prevalence of comorbidities, stratified by age, sex and race/ethnicity, from NHANES. We describe medical costs and quality of life decrements associated with obesity in the Supplementary Material (1.1B). In scenarios without bariatric surgeries, an individual’s minimum BMI was 30 kg/m2, but in scenarios including surgeries, the minimum BMI was 35 kg/m2, to ensure all individuals were eligible for interventions under consideration.

#### Weight-loss Regimen Characteristics

We summarize efficacy, adverse events and cost details for the diet and exercise and bariatric surgery regimens in the Supplementary Material (Section 1.2B/F) (15–17).

#### Treatment Characteristics: Semaglutide (Table 1)

We derived 2-year weight-loss associated with semaglutide from the STEP-5 and STEP-2 trials (21, 42). Table 1 shows the mean weight-loss for someone with and without diabetes (21, 42).

We used data from WE-CAN to set the pain reduction associated with specific weight-loss levels, which ranged from 35–50% (12, 15). We validated pain reduction in the model with data from the STEP-9 trial (SM, Table A11). For individuals with diabetes, we used STEP-2 data to derive a 68% probability of remission (42). We set type 2 diabetes incidence at 27% of the baseline rate (43). In the model, individuals on semaglutide experienced a 20% reduction in MACE risk (44).

We derived the probability of minor semaglutide-related adverse events from STEP-5 (6.6%, SM, 1.2C) (21). Using published data, we estimated that 20.5% of semaglutide users discontinued treatment in the first year and 3.1% discontinued thereafter (45–56). Details are presented in the Supplementary Material (1.2C).

We estimated annual costs of semaglutide ($8,585 and $4,273, without or with diabetes) using the US Office of Health Policy-reported net prices of the medication plus costs of lifestyle coaching ($792/year) (57).

#### Treatment Characteristics: Tirzepatide (Table 1)

We derived weight-loss for tirzepatide from SURMOUNT-4 and SURMOUNT-2 (Table 1) (58, 59). As with semaglutide, weight-loss was lower for people with diabetes. Pain reduction associated with weight-loss was from WE-CAN (15). For those with diabetes at baseline, 79% experienced remission (59). We set type 2 diabetes incidence at 7% of the baseline rate (60). The probability of minor tirzepatide-related adverse events was from SURMOUNT-1 (6.9%, SM, 1.2D) (22). We estimated the annual cost of tirzepatide ($10,508 and $4,292, without or with diabetes) using the US Office of Health Policy-reported net prices of the medication plus lifestyle coaching ($792/year) (57).

### Assumptions

We based the analysis on several assumptions: 1) We did not limit the duration for which individuals could use GLP1RAs. 2) Weight-loss was maintained throughout the GLP1RA use period, but treatment discontinuation caused all lost weight to be regained over two years, as trials have shown significant regain effects within even one year of discontinuation (58, 61). 3) MACE risk reduction and discontinuation rates were similar for tirzepatide and semaglutide (62). 4) Greater weight-loss led to more pain relief for non-surgical interventions (9, 40, 41). For a given BMI reduction, we assumed similar pain relief for GLP1RAs compared to the diet and exercise intervention. We used LABS data to derive pain relief for bariatric surgery and assumed that surgery type did not independently impact relief level (63).

### Model Validation

To assess model validity, we compared OAPol estimates for the BMI reduction of each intervention to published findings (SM, Table A11). We validated OAPol-estimated pain reduction from semaglutide use with STEP-9 trial results (SM, Table A11, Figure A2). The modeled pain reduction trajectories from Diet and Exercise regimen and bariatric surgeries have been previously published (15, 17). Finally, we compared MACE risk reduction from semaglutide in the SELECT trial to the estimated risk reduction in the OAPol model (SM, Table A11).

### Sensitivity Analyses

#### Deterministic Sensitivity Analyses

We performed one- and two-way sensitivity analyses, varying inputs for the cohort, tirzepatide, and semaglutide characteristics (SM, Table A9). Variations for the cohort characteristics included: initial BMI (33 – 54 kg/m2), starting age (46 – 66), starting pain (20 – 71), annual medical costs for class I/II/III obesity (+/− 2SD from base case), the quality-of-life decrement associated with class III obesity (0 – 0.075 QALYs), sex distribution (100% female – 100% male), race distribution (100% White – 100% Black) and discount rate (0 – 5%). Variations in tirzepatide-related parameters included: maximum duration (5 years - lifetime), BMI reduction efficacy (50% - 150% of base case), pain reduction efficacy (50% - 150% of base case), cost (50% – 150% of base case), diabetes remission (50% - 100%), diabetes incidence (0 – 100% of base rate), minor adverse event risk (0% - 200% of base case), discontinuation rate (0.5x – 2x of base case) and MACE risk reduction (0% - 30%). We varied the amount of pain relief in D+E regimen in two ways: 1) giving everybody regardless of weight loss the pain benefit (32% reduction, as reported by WE-CAN trial), 2) not giving any pain benefit for those on D+E regimen who did not achieve weight loss >5%.

In two-way deterministic sensitivity analyses, we varied the most influential parameters from the one-way analysis. The combinations of parameters are presented in the SM (1.3A). We only considered non-surgical strategies in these analyses. We also conducted analyses examining time horizon, diet and exercise MACE reduction and starting KL OA grades (SM 2.6).

#### Probabilistic Sensitivity Analyses

We performed a probabilistic sensitivity analysis, simultaneously varying parameters in 1,000 simulations of 1 million individuals for all weight-loss strategies (28, 64). We present the probability distributions used in the Supplementary Material (Table A10). The results are presented in cost-effectiveness acceptability curves, displaying the probability a strategy was cost-effective at thresholds from $0 - $200,000/QALY. We conducted this analysis both without and with bariatric surgeries available.

## Results

### Base Case Analysis

In the primary analysis focused on non-surgical options (minimum BMI set to 30 kg/m2) conducted from the healthcare perspective, UC led to 9.59 QALYs compared to 9.75 for diet and exercise, 10.48 for semaglutide and 10.68 for tirzepatide. Lifetime costs were estimated at $222,300, $226,300, $273,500 and $280,000 for UC and the three weight-loss strategies (Table 2). When analyzed incrementally (comparing an intervention to the one with next-lowest cost), adding diet and exercise to UC resulted in an ICER of $25,400/QALY, while adding tirzepatide produced an ICER of $57,400/QALY (Table 2). Tirzepatide dominated semaglutide, meaning it provided greater clinical benefits at lower costs. When each strategy was compared against usual care, diet and exercise and tirzepatide had absolute cost-effectiveness ratios of $25,400/QALY and $52,800/QALY, respectively (Table 2). Results from the societal perspective were qualitatively similar (SM, Table A15).

In the secondary analysis, in simulations with everybody eligible for bariatric surgery, adding LSG to UC resulted in an ICER of $20,600/QALY and dominated diet and exercise. Compared to LSG, RYGB yielded an ICER of $30,700/QALY and dominated semaglutide and tirzepatide (Table 2).

### One-Way Sensitivity Analyses

Tirzepatide’s ICER was most sensitive to changes in weight-loss efficacy and treatment costs (Figure 2). When tirzepatide’s BMI reduction was 50–75% of the base case, semaglutide dominated tirzepatide. Tirzepatide’s ICER increased to $153,800/QALY when using Federal Supply Schedule costs and decreased to $18,600/QALY at a cost of 50% the net price. Lowering the cohort BMI to 33 kg/m2 and eliminating MACE risk reduction abilities also caused the ICER to increase substantially. Varying demographic characteristics (age, sex and race) and other intervention parameters did not lead to meaningful changes.

Results of the sensitivity analyses giving everybody on D+E regimen the same amount of pain relief or eliminating the chance of pain relief for those who did not achieve weight reduction >5% did not meaningfully affect the ICER for tirzepatide (corresponding ICERs are $57,100/QALY and $56,300/QALY, respectively) compared to $57,400 in the base case.

### Two-Way Sensitivity Analyses

Figure 3 displays results of four two-way sensitivity analyses varying the cost of tirzepatide against (A) BMI reduction, (B) maximum use duration, (C) mean cohort BMI, and (D) semaglutide cost in scenarios without bariatric surgery. Tirzepatide’s ICER was above $100,000/QALY or dominated when annual cost was at or above the base case cost and the BMI reduction efficacy was −25% or −50% the base case efficacy. Tirzepatide ICERs were below $100,000 regardless of maximum use duration, except when the cost was 150% of the base case. A “U-shaped” curve was present when varying cohort BMI; both low BMIs (33 kg/m2) and high BMIs (54 kg/m2) led to ICERs above $100,000/QALY when annual cost was ≥125% the base case. Decreases in semaglutide cost in concert with increases in tirzepatide cost shifted tirzepatide’s ICER above $100,000/QALY and semaglutide’s below $50,000/QALY (SM, Figure A7). Results varying semaglutide inputs are available in the SM (2.5).

### Probabilistic Sensitivity Analyses

With a cost-effectiveness threshold of $100,000/QALY, tirzepatide was cost-effective in 64% of simulations and semaglutide in 34% (Figure 4A). When including surgeries and increasing the minimum BMI to 35 kg/m2, RYGB was cost-effective in 68% and LSG in 17% of scenarios when the threshold was $100,000/QALY (Figure 4B).

## Discussion

We evaluated the cost-effectiveness of adding GLP1RA medications and other weight-loss strategies for managing patients with knee OA and obesity. We found that tirzepatide dominated semaglutide and would be cost-effective for payers with cost-effectiveness thresholds above $57,400/QALY, when added to usual care. Diet and exercise could be a cost-effective strategy for payers with more limited thresholds of $25,400 – $57,400/QALY. Examining the value of GLP1RAs among those who would be eligible for both non-surgical and surgical regimens, we found that RYGB would offer the best return on investment for cost-effectiveness thresholds above $30,700/QALY. The favorable cost-effectiveness of bariatric surgery may stem from the long-term weight maintenance that the procedures provide for a single up-front cost compared to a recurring, high annual cost for the GLP1RA medications.

The ICERs for semaglutide and tirzepatide were sensitive to changes in annual costs. Reducing the annual cost of tirzepatide to 75% of base case would make it cost-effective for a wide range of BMIs, treatment durations, and weight-loss efficacies. Notably, semaglutide became cost-effective for payers with thresholds between $40,500 - $120,300/QALY when the annual cost was reduced 25% from the base case (SM, Figure A7), demonstrating how cost drives the relative value of these strategies. Competition between GLP1RA manufacturers or payer negotiations could potentially drive down the price of the drugs to further improve their value. Semaglutide’s Medicare Part D negotiated prices due to the Inflation Reduction Act are scheduled to take effect in 2027, which may also lower prices (65).

A U-shaped trend emerged in sensitivity analyses varying average cohort BMI. As starting BMI decreased below 40 kg/m2, the ability for diet and exercise to move someone out of each obesity class approached that of GLP1RAs, making the medications less comparatively effective. However, at higher BMI (>47 kg/m2), tirzepatide became less likely to offer weight-loss benefits that would alter obesity class, so the beneficial impact was reduced relative to diet and exercise.

These findings add to evidence from previous research on the cost-effectiveness of GLP1RA medications, diet and exercise programs, and bariatric surgery procedures (15–18, 24, 66–70). A recent study compared semaglutide and tirzepatide to two other anti-obesity medications and lifestyle modification alone and found that tirzepatide would only be cost-effective at a cost-effectiveness threshold >$200,000/QALY, while semaglutide would require a threshold >$470,000/QALY (70). Compared to each other, tirzepatide would dominate semaglutide. Other studies have found that tirzepatide could be cost-effective compared to semaglutide at a threshold of $100,000/QALY, and that both dominated liraglutide, an older GLP1RA (24, 68, 69). GLP1RAs had ICERs >$300,000/QALY compared to phentermine + topiramate, and another study showed semaglutide had an ICER of $122,500/QALY compared to a diet and exercise intervention (24, 67, 68). Our more favorable results for GLP1RAs in the absence of surgery could reflect the additional benefits from reducing knee OA pain, and/or our use of net drug prices, which are generally lower than the wholesale acquisition costs used in some prior studies. Future decreases in GLP1RA pricing may also contribute to favorable results. While non-GLP1RA medications such as phentermine-topiramate (costing about 80% less than GLP1RAs) have been shown to be cost-effective, our decision to exclude them from the current analysis was based on their low uptake and lack of data in a population with OA (70, 71).

Prior studies have shown that diet and exercise regimens added to usual OA care could be cost-effective compared to UC alone, with ICERs between $30,000-$40,000/QALY (15, 18). The $25,400/QALY ICER for diet and exercise versus UC in the current analysis is consistent with published literature (15, 18). Other studies have also estimated ICERs <$25,000/QALY for LSG and RYGB when compared to usual care for patients with OA and morbid obesity, which is in line with our results.

Published literature is not consistent with respect to the magnitude of pain relief among people with OA achieving a small (<5%) BMI reduction. Results from cohort studies show that the pain reduction is greater than 0 but lower than the minimally clinically important difference (MCID) for WOMAC pain (~10 points on 0–100 scale) (9). Data from clinical trials point to pain relief consistent with the MCID (40). Our extensive sensitivity analyses showed that the cost-effectiveness of tirzepatide was robust to assumptions regarding the relationship between BMI reduction and pain reduction.

Despite its low ICER, the diet and exercise intervention would not be considered optimal from the cost-effectiveness perspective for thresholds greater than $57,400/QALY, as it offers fewer clinical benefits than tirzepatide. Including diet and exercise as a comparator showed that even if diet and exercise is available, tirzepatide offers a better value by maximizing clinical benefits for cost-effectiveness thresholds above 57,400/QALY.

We note several limitations. With limited data on long-term GLP1RA weight-loss efficacy, adherence or adverse events, we assumed a lifetime use duration (with a higher first year discontinuation probability and lower for subsequent years) in which weight-loss was maintained for the entire time an individual was taking the medication. These results are based on current data and thus do not account for potential future developments in long-term GLP1RA weight-maintenance effectiveness or adverse events. Despite this limitation, decreasing the duration of tirzepatide use to a maximum of five years lowered its ICER to $30,100/QALY, which would not have qualitatively changed our conclusions regarding its cost-effectiveness. We also assumed that conditional on the amount of weight-loss, GLP1RA interventions would provide similar pain relief to diet and exercise. This simplified assumption may omit pain reduction arising from non-BMI-related processes. Furthermore, the OAPol model structure necessitates discontinuation of GLP1RAs following a MACE. Since only 14% of those taking GLP1RAs discontinue due to MACEs in the model, this limitation is not likely to meaningfully impact the results.

We conducted extensive sensitivity analyses, which showed that costs, weight-loss efficacy and cohort starting BMI influenced tirzepatide cost-effectiveness, while the probability of adverse events associated with GLP1RA use, and pain reduction associated with weight-loss did not substantially impact ICERs. Additionally, pharmacological weight-loss has been linked to muscle mass loss, but we did not include this as an adverse event due to a lack of evidence indicating it may cause physical frailty or sarcopenia. Finally, the societal perspective only considered indirect costs from knee pain and TKR and not from productivity reductions due to undergoing bariatric surgery. Given the focus on individual weight-loss strategies in this analysis, future research could examine the value of consecutive or combined weight-loss interventions.

As nearly 30 million people in the US have knee OA and many of those individuals have BMI >30kg/m2, weight-loss could lead to large quality-of-life benefits due to improvements in knee pain and function (1, 7, 8, 10–13). Our findings suggest that, when added to usual OA care, tirzepatide use could optimize resource allocation for patients ineligible for or unwilling to pursue bariatric surgery for payers with cost-effectiveness thresholds above $57,400/QALY. Given the choice between GLP1RAs, tirzepatide would be more economically attractive than semaglutide at current net prices. However, payers may want to consider negotiated medication prices for tirzepatide and semaglutide in their decision making. For individuals who are clinically eligible and interested in undergoing surgery, surgical intervention could be a cost-effective treatment strategy. This direct comparison between prescription medication and bariatric surgery may assist policy makers in setting policy recommendations related to treatment options for people with knee OA and obesity who would be eligible for both surgical and non-surgical interventions. Clinicians may consider discussing the differences between these weight-loss interventions, their potential benefits and harms, and currently available knee OA care options with their eligible patients.
